messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was sixty-two when the accident happened, a man who had worked at First National for thirty-eight years without incident. He prided himself on steadiness, on being the reliable presence customers recognized when they came through his line. On a Tuesday in March, a regular customer—a woman in her seventies named Mrs. Chen—approached his window during the lunch rush. She was retrieving a cashier's check, and Marcus, moving quickly to keep the queue moving, reached across the counter to hand it to her. In that moment, his elbow caught the edge of a water bottle she had set on the counter. It fell directly onto her foot, and she screamed. What followed was a cascade of terrible clarity: the woman's ankle had fractured badly, the ambulance, the manager's concerned face, the knowledge that this had happened because he was rushing, because he hadn't been careful enough. Mrs. Chen spent six weeks in a boot. Marcus spent the time after replaying those two seconds—the bottle falling, her cry—over and over, each time feeling the same sickening weight of responsibility.

The months that followed were marked by a slow, creeping erosion of how Marcus understood himself. When his wife Sarah touched him unexpectedly—a hand on his shoulder as she passed his chair, a gentle tap on his arm to get his attention—he would flinch violently, his body rigid until he recognized it was her. The surprise of touch had become intolerable, a reminder that he could not be trusted to notice what was happening around him, that his awareness had failed Mrs. Chen. He had come to believe he was fundamentally inadequate, that something essential had broken in him that day. His reactions since the accident—the jumpiness, the way he could no longer simply relax even on weekends when he was objectively safe at home—proved to him that he was a lousy coper, someone who couldn't manage his own mind. These convictions deepened whenever he encountered stress of any kind, or when he saw people who reminded him of Mrs. Chen, or even when a relative called unexpectedly. Each trigger reinforced his sense of permanent damage, as though the accident had fundamentally altered who he was.

At night, Marcus lay awake beside Sarah, his mind alert and scanning. He had convinced himself that he needed to stay vigilant, that sleep was a luxury he no longer deserved, that something catastrophic would happen if he let his guard down. The vigilance was exhausting, but it felt necessary—a penance of sorts. When fragments of the memory surfaced without warning—the bottle tilting, the sound of her pain—the terror he felt was identical to what he had experienced in that moment at the counter. His heart would race, his hands would sweat, and the guilt would wash over him with the same intensity as the day it happened. These memories seemed to appear randomly, uninvited, and then dissolve just as suddenly, leaving him shaken and unsure of what had triggered them. The unpredictability of these intrusions kept him on edge, hyperalert to any sign that the memory might return.

What had begun as guilt about a specific accident had metastasized into a conviction that he was permanently changed for the worse. The threat he felt was not merely about another accident—it was about the truth he believed the accident had revealed: that he was unreliable, that his mind could not be trusted. This belief made him acutely sensitive to any moment of stress or any encounter with people who resembled his regular customers, because each one felt like a test he was destined to fail. The hypervigilance and the insomnia had become his constant companions, and they fed the memory, which in turn fed the conviction that he was a bad coper, a man who had lost something irreplaceable on that ordinary Tuesday. After eight months of this, Marcus finally told Sarah that he needed help. He was terrified that nothing could undo what he had become, but he was more terrified of continuing to live as he was—trapped in the certainty of his own inadequacy, unable to sleep, unable to accept a touch from the woman he loved without flinching away.
